newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Iberian bonds spread to slip a bit by Dec.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Iberian bonds spread to slip a bit by Dec.

text.p: Investors will turn a more critical on Spain and Portugal's convergence chances this year, and although bonds could continue to out sprint core markets, the euphoric rush to Iberia has drawn to a close.

Spanish and Portuguese 10-year benchmark bonds will shave their yield spreads versus the German core market in one year to an average of around 70 basis points and 65 basis points, respectively, according to a Reuter survey of 11 analysts.
On Tuesday, the spreads, which reflect how risky the market sees Spanish and Portuguese bonds, traded around 90 basis points for Spain and 88 for Portugal.

The Spanish spread has narrowed from 330 basis points since last March and the Portuguese from 320 points on expectations the two nations will help launch the single European currency in 1999. If the two countries participate as expected, the spreads must narrow close to zero by 1999.
But the survey, conducted from January 21 to 23, revealed a wide disparity in views despite the average forecast for falls.
Analysts contributed a wide range, with a maximum for the spread in one year of 120 basis points and a low of 40 basis points on both markets.

Banco Cisf in Lisbon, whose expectations are in line with the poll's average for year end, expected the spread to rebound and end the third quarter around 115 basis points in Spain and 105 basis points in Portugal.
But by year end, spreads should narrow again to about 75 basis points on both markets, it said.

"Even given a 100 percent probability of Spain and Portugal entering EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) from its start, a spread at any level from 75 basis points to 100 basis points is normal because of exchange rate risk," said a Banco Cisf analyst.
Even the most optimistic forecasts among those polled, showed the 10-year Iberian yield spread over Bunds cannot slide by more than 40 basis points.
"The EMU project will go on. Even if we have a short delay in the entry, the market will continue to consider with favour Spain's possibilities," said Giovanni Polastri, economist at 4CAST in London.
"At this point, the market will trade at around 40 to 50 basis points, which is a fair level, given a credit risk at around zero and considering only currency risk," Polastri said.
But some of those polled predicted the market will soon reevaluate its optimistic stance toward the two countries.
Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America here, expected the spread to soon reverse and widen steadily toward 120 basis points by year end.
"We'll have divergence instead," Lumholdt said.

"The market will realise Spain is not ready yet, and it will also start to see that if Spain is allowed to enter then, Italy also has to be in...This is going to be very hard to sell to German public opinion," he said.
For Portugal, Bank Essi in Lisbon also expected the spread to trade back toward 120 basis points by December.

Further out into 1998, the Reuters poll shows less volatile forecasts, with the larger Iberian market earning lower marks with a likely spread over Bunds of about 50 basis points. The Portguese spread is seen near 30 basis points.
Portugual's spreads are seen between 10 and 30 basis points.
But the Spanish spread is seen very volatile, with forecasts ranging from 10 basis points to 150 basis points.
